items.question: What makes materials science and CuspAI the kind of work you want to pursue at this stage of your career?
items.object: Materials science and CuspAI as a choice of research direction
items.answer: Working in two-dimensional quantum gravity, you're pretty much guaranteed there's going to be no impact on what you do—maybe a few papers, but not in this world at this energy scale. As I get closer to retirement, which is fortunately still 10 years away or so, I do want to kind of make a positive impact in the world. And I got pretty worried about climate change. Politics seems to have a hard time solving it, especially these days. So I thought, better work on it from the technology side, and that's why we started CuspAI. But there's also a lot of really interesting science problems in material science, and so it's kind of combining both the impact you can make with it as well as the interesting science. So it's sort of these two dimensions: working on things which you feel is like, wow, there's something very deep going on here, and on the other hand trying to build tools that can actually make a real impact in the world.

items.question: How do you see physics as the thread connecting your work on symmetries and machine learning?
items.object: Physics and the role of symmetries in machine learning
items.answer: Yeah, I think physics is the thread. So, having spent a lot of time in theoretical physics, I think there's first very fundamental and exciting questions, like things that haven't actually been figured out in quantum gravity. So there's really the frontier, but there's also a lot of mathematical tools that you can use, right? In, for instance, particle physics, but also in general relativity, symmetry spaces play an enormously important role. And this goes all the way to gauge symmetries as well. And so applying these kinds of symmetries to machine learning was actually, you know, I thought of it as a very deep and interesting mathematical problem. I did this with Taco Cohen, and Taco was the main driver behind this. It went all the way from just simple rotational symmetries all the way to gauge symmetries on spheres and stuff like that. And Maurice Weiler, who's also here, when he was a PhD student with me, wrote an entire book, which I can really recommend, about the role of symmetries in AI and machine learning, that I find is a very deep and interesting problem.

items.question: Why does the connection between diffusion models and stochastic thermodynamics excite you?
items.object: The connection between diffusion models and stochastic thermodynamics
items.answer: So more recently, I've taken a sort of different path, which is the relationship between diffusion models and a field called stochastic thermodynamics. This is basically thermodynamics, which is a theory of equilibrium, but then formulated for out-of-equilibrium systems. And it turns out that the mathematics that we use for diffusion models, but even for reinforcement learning, for Schrödinger bridges, for MCMC sampling, has the same mathematics as this physical theory of non-equilibrium systems. And that got me very excited. Actually, when I taught a course in South Africa, close to Cape Town, at the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences, I turned that into a book. So two years later, the book is finished. I've sent it to the publisher, and this is about the deep relationship between free energy, diffusion models, basically generative AI, and stochastic thermodynamics. So it's always some kind of—I don't know, I find physics very deep.

items.question: How do you view your PhD advisor’s attempt to develop a more understandable theory of quantum mechanics?
items.object: His PhD advisor’s attempt to make quantum mechanics understandable
items.answer: I did my PhD with a Nobel laureate, the brilliant man I've ever met. He was never wrong about anything as long as I've seen him, and now he says quantum mechanics is wrong and he has a new theory of quantum mechanics. Nobody understands what he's saying, even though what he's writing down is not mathematically very complex. But he's trying to address this understandability, let's say, of quantum mechanics head-on. I find it very courageous, and I'm completely fascinated by it. So I'm also trying to think about, okay, can I actually understand quantum mechanics in a more mundane way, without all the weird multiverses and collapses and stuff like that?

items.question: Why do you see materials as such a fundamental opportunity to make an impact through AI for science?
items.object: Materials as a foundation for technological progress
items.answer: So my view is that underlying almost everything is a material. There's the LLM; underlying it is a GPU on which it runs, and then in order to make that GPU, you have to put materials down on a wafer and shine on it with EUV light in order to etch the structures in. But that's now an actual material problem because more or less we've reached the limits of scaling things down, and now we are trying to improve further by new materials. So that's a fundamental materials problem. We need to get through the energy transition fast if we don't want to mess up this world.

items.question: Why do you see removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as essential to addressing climate change?
items.object: Atmospheric carbon dioxide removal as a response to climate change
items.answer: I'm still worried about climate change. I realized that in order to stay within two degrees, let's say, we would not only have to reduce our emissions to zero by 2050, but then another half century or even a century of removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, not by reducing your emissions but actually removing it at a rate that's about half the rate that we now emit it. And that is an unsolved problem. If we don't solve it, 2° is not going to happen; it's going to be much more. And I don't think people quite understand how bad that can be, like four degrees. Very bad.

items.question: How do you think about the design of your materials discovery platform?
items.object: The design of a materials discovery platform combining a digital twin, experiments, and agents
items.answer: We have a digital twin which walks through the steps of the ladder. They do the cheap things first, weed out everything that's obviously useless, and then go to more and more expensive things later. And so you narrow things down to a small number; those go into an experiment, you do the experiment, get feedback, etc. Now, things that have also been more recently added are more agentic parts. We have agents that search the literature and come up with chemical suggestions or suggestions for doing experiments. We have agents which autonomously orchestrate all of the computations and experiments that need to be done. They're in various stages of maturity and can be continuously improved, I would say. So that's basically—I don't think that part is rocket science, the design of that thing.

items.question: How do you weigh data augmentation against hardcoding equivariance into a neural network?
items.object: Data augmentation versus hardcoded equivariance in neural networks
items.answer: Now I have to say, sometimes data augmentation works even better than hardcoding the equivariances in. This has to do with the fact that if you constrain the weights before the optimization starts, the optimization surface or objective becomes more complicated, and so it's harder to find good minima. So there is also a complicated interplay, I think, between the optimization process and these constraints you put in your network. You'll hear contradicting claims in this field: for certain applications, some people say it works just better than not doing it; sometimes you hear other people say if you have a lot of data and can do data augmentation, then it's easier to optimize and it actually works better than putting the equivariances in.

items.question: How do you think the bitter lesson about scale applies to neural networks that incorporate symmetry?
items.object: The bitter lesson for symmetry-based neural networks
items.answer: You know, the symmetry is there. It's hard to imagine there isn't a way to actually leverage it. But yeah, so there is a bitter lesson. One of the bitter lessons is you should always make sure you architect your scale, unless you have a tiny data set, in which case it doesn't matter. But the same bitter lessons you can draw in LLM space are eventually going to be true in this space as well, I think.

items.question: What do you find exciting about the connection your book Generative AI and Stochastic Thermodynamics draws between machine learning and physics?
items.object: Generative AI and Stochastic Thermodynamics, Max Welling's book
items.answer: This book is called Generative AI and Stochastic Thermodynamics. It basically lays bare the fact that the mathematics that goes into both generative AI, which is the technology to generate images and videos, and this field of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, which is systems of molecules that are moving around and relaxing to their ground state or that you can control to be in a certain state, is actually identical. And so that's fascinating. In fact, what's interesting is that Jeff Hinton and Radford Neal already wrote down the variational free energy for machine learning a long time ago. And there's also Carl Friston's work on the free energy principle and active inference. But now we've related it to this very new field in physics called stochastic thermodynamics or non-equilibrium thermodynamics, which has its own very interesting theorems, like fluctuation theorems, which we don't typically talk about but can learn a lot from. I think it can start to cross-fertilize. When we see that these things are actually the same, we can, like we did for symmetries, look at this new theory developed by these very smart physicists and say, okay, what can we take from here that will make our algorithms better? At the same time, we can use our models to help the scientists do better science. And so it becomes a beautiful cross-fertilization between these two fields. The book is rather technical, I would say, and it takes all sorts of things that have been done in stochastic thermodynamics and all sorts of models that have been done in the machine learning literature and basically equates them to each other. I think hopefully that sense of unification will be revealing to people.
